messages.subject: Model does not contain any samples, network meta-analysis
parts:
Hello,

I'm starting to learn Stan and I thought I would begin by trying to convert WinBUGS code from here (http://www.nicedsu.org.uk/evidence-synthesis-tsd-series(2391675).htm) into Stan code.  I started with the TSD2-1 files and have run into problems with 1c. The WinBUGS code is this (taken from the .odc file I've attached):

# Binomial likelihood, logit link
# Random effects model for multi-arm trials
model{                               # *** PROGRAM STARTS
for(i in 1:ns){                      # LOOP THROUGH STUDIES
    w[i,1] <- 0    # adjustment for multi-arm trials is zero for control arm
    delta[i,1] <- 0             # treatment effect is zero for control arm
    mu[i] ~ dnorm(0,.0001)           # vague priors for all trial baselines
    for (k in 1:na[i]) {             # LOOP THROUGH ARMS
        r[i,k] ~ dbin(p[i,k],n[i,k]) # binomial likelihood
        logit(p[i,k]) <- mu[i] + delta[i,k]  # model for linear predictor
        rhat[i,k] <- p[i,k] * n[i,k] # expected value of the numerators 
#Deviance contribution
        dev[i,k] <- 2 * (r[i,k] * (log(r[i,k])-log(rhat[i,k]))  
            +  (n[i,k]-r[i,k]) * (log(n[i,k]-r[i,k]) - log(n[i,k]-rhat[i,k])))         }
#  summed residual deviance contribution for this trial
    resdev[i] <- sum(dev[i,1:na[i]])       
    for (k in 2:na[i]) {             # LOOP THROUGH ARMS
# trial-specific LOR distributions
        delta[i,k] ~ dnorm(md[i,k],taud[i,k])
# mean of LOR distributions (with multi-arm trial correction)
        md[i,k] <-  d[t[i,k]] - d[t[i,1]] + sw[i,k]
# precision of LOR distributions (with multi-arm trial correction)
        taud[i,k] <- tau *2*(k-1)/k
# adjustment for multi-arm RCTs
        w[i,k] <- (delta[i,k] - d[t[i,k]] + d[t[i,1]])
# cumulative adjustment for multi-arm trials
        sw[i,k] <- sum(w[i,1:k-1])/(k-1)
      }
  }   
totresdev <- sum(resdev[])           # Total Residual Deviance
d[1]<-0       # treatment effect is zero for reference treatment
# vague priors for treatment effects
for (k in 2:nt){  d[k] ~ dnorm(0,.0001) }
sd ~ dunif(0,5)     # vague prior for between-trial SD
tau <- pow(sd,-2)   # between-trial precision = (1/between-trial variance)
# Provide estimates of treatment effects T[k] on the natural (probability) scale
# Given a Mean Effect, meanA, for 'standard' treatment A, 
# with precision (1/variance) precA
A ~ dnorm(meanA,precA)
for (k in 1:nt) { logit(T[k]) <- A + d[k]  }
}                                    # *** PROGRAM ENDS                          

My attempted Stan code is this: 

data {
  int<lower=0> ND; // Number of data points
  int<lower=0> NT; // Number of treatments
  int<lower=0> NS; // Number of studies
  int<lower=0> sampleSize[ND]; // Number of patients in study and treatment arm 
  int<lower=0> responders[ND]; // Number of responders in study and treatment arm
  int<lower=1> treatment[ND]; // Treatment used in study and treatment arm
  int<lower=1> study[ND]; // Study for data point
  int<lower=1> treatment_base[ND]; // The first or control treatment per study
} 
parameters {
  vector[NT] d;
  vector[NS] mu;
  real delta[NS,NT];
  real<lower=0> sigmasq_delta; 
  real delta_new;
}
transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma_delta;
  matrix[NS,NT] w;
  matrix[NS,NT] sw;
//  matrix[NS,NT] md;
//  matrix[NS,NT] vard;
//  matrix[NS,NT] sqrt_vard; 
  sigma_delta <- sqrt(sigmasq_delta);
  for (i in 1:ND) {
    if (treatment[i] == 1) {
 w[study[i],treatment[i]] <- 0.0; // adjustment for multi-arm trials is zero for control arm
    } else {
 // adjustment for multi-arm RCTs
      w[study[i],treatment[i]] <- delta[study[i],treatment[i]] - d[treatment[i]] + d[treatment_base[i]];
 // cumulative adjustment for multi-arm RCTs
      sw[study[i],treatment[i]] <- sum(w[study[i],1:(treatment[i]-1)])/(treatment[i]-1);
    }
//  md[study[i],treatment[i]] <- d[treatment[i]] - d[treatment_base[i]] + sw[study[i],treatment[i]];
//        vard[study[i],treatment[i]] <- (pow(sigmasq_delta, 2) * treatment[i])./(2 * (treatment[i]-1));
//  sqrt_vard[study[i],treatment[i]] <- sqrt(vard[study[i],treatment[i]]);
  }
}  
model {
  for (i in 1:ND) {
    if (treatment[i] == 1) {
   responders[i] ~ binomial_logit(sampleSize[i], mu[study[i]]);
} else {
      responders[i] ~ binomial_logit(sampleSize[i], mu[study[i]] + delta[study[i],treatment[i]]);
}
delta[study[i],treatment[i]] ~ student_t(4,d[treatment[i]],sigma_delta);
//  delta[study[i],treatment[i]] ~ normal(md[study[i],treatment[i]],sqrt_vard[study[i],treatment[i]]);
mu[study[i]] ~ normal(0, sqrt(1E5));
    d[treatment[i]] ~ normal(0, sqrt(1E5)); 
    sigmasq_delta ~ inv_gamma(1E-2, 1E-2); 
  }
}

The problems seems to center around the calculation of sw for the multi-arm adjustment, so I've commented out the md, vard, sqrt_vard calculation until that gets dealt with.  If I comment out the sw line I can get samples from the model.  If I define sw as just sum(w[study[i],1:(treatment[i]-1)]) or just 1/(treatment[i]-1) I get samples from the model, but as-is the model seems to fail. I've attached the data I use in Rda and txt files.

Can anyone see what would cause Stan to output that "Stan model 'TSD2-1cRE_Bi_logit' does not contain samples."? Am I doing something fundamentally wrong?

And, since I'm still learning, is there anything else that anyone would suggest to improve the code?

Thank you,
Richard

legal (too bad it doesn't say that explicitly) or some other error
arose during sampling (like illegal generated quantities).

I'm not sure if this is of interest to anyone, but maybe it can help someone else avoid errors.

The problem was that I was only populating part of the "w" array and then summing over a whole row/column.  I didn't initialize the array to be full of zeroes, though, so it failed all the time.  I would look at values output from the summing over "w" but that only included the samples that succeeded.  After I added a print statement the errors popped up and things were pretty clear.

I initialized the matrix with a "w <- rep_array(0.0, NS, NT);" statement and it's running fine, but slow.

I'm not sure if I should start a new topic, but I'm trying to vectorize the model now.  I'd like to do something like... "y[1:ND] ~ normal(a[study[1:ND]] + b[study[1:ND], treatment[1:ND]], se[1:ND]);" and "w[study[1:ND], treatment[1:ND]] <- delta[study[1:ND],treatment[1:ND] - d[treatment[1:ND]];" where ND is the number of data points and study and treatment are vectors containing the corresponding study and treatment for each data point, but I suspect that won't quite work... an array like b[study[1:ND], treatment[1:ND]] will not behave like a vector b[1:ND], right?  Any idea if I can do something different to vectorize?

Thanks,
Richard

Either way's OK.
> I'd like to do something like... "y[1:ND] ~ normal(a[study[1:ND]] + b[study[1:ND], treatment[1:ND]], se[1:ND]);"

This doesn't make sense as there's only two arguments to normal. And if
"se" is for "standard error", you probably don't mean that. The std err
is a measure of estimator accuracy. We just use sigma or tau.

To answer your question, yes you can do what you want to do:

I'm going to ignore that treatment thing because I don' tknow what it is,
but you can program a model with two varying intercepts as

y ~ normal(a[study] + b[study], sigma);

assuming y, study, and sigma are all the same size N, so that it's equal to

for (n in 1:N)
y[n] ~ normal(a[study[n]] + b[study[n]], sigma[n]);

It'll also work if sigma is a scalar (in which case sigma[n] becomes sigma above).
You don't usually have a varying scale for each observation because you can't
can't be fit with a single observation.

> and "w[study[1:ND], treatment[1:ND]] <- delta[study[1:ND],treatment[1:ND] - d[treatment[1:ND]];" where ND is the number of data points and study and treatment are vectors containing the corresponding study and treatment for each data point, but I suspect that won't quite work... an array like b[study[1:ND], treatment[1:ND]] will not behave like a vector b[1:ND], right? Any idea if I can do something different to vectorize?

See the indexing section of the manual for full details.
If a is a vector and nn is an array of integers, then
a[nn] is a vector of the same size as the array nn. And so
on for other types.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Model does not contain any samples, network meta-analysis
parts:
I see. No, there's no good way to vectorize that as a one-liner.

The basic idea is that if you have multiple indexes, Stan's indexing
works as:

b[study, value2][i,j] = b[study[i], value2[j]]

So b[study, value2] is of the same type as b (e.g., real[,] or matrix).

That's the same way that R works, by the way:

> a <- matrix(1:6, 2, 3)

> a
[,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,] 1 3 5
[2,] 2 4 6

> a[c(1,2), c(2,3)]
[,1] [,2]
[1,] 3 5
[2,] 4 6

Now if it's a square matrix, you could use

diag(b[study, value]),

but it wouldn't be efficient. Just use loops to define the value you want.

real b[N];

...
for (n in 1:N)

b_sv[n] <- b[study[n], value[n]];

... use b_study_value ...

- Bob
